passages.happening:
The chapter is a list of every place Israel camped between Egypt and the Jordan. Moses wrote it down ‘at the LORD’s command’ (verse 2).

It begins on the day after the first Passover. “They marched out defiantly in full view of all the Egyptians, who were burying all their firstborn” (verses 3-4). Then it goes stage by stage, each in the same words: they set out from one place and camped at another. It passes the sea, Marah and Elim, the wilderness of Sinai, Kadesh and Mount Hor (verses 5-37).

At Mount Hor it stops for a moment. “At the LORD’s command, Aaron the priest climbed Mount Hor and died there on the first day of the fifth month, in the fortieth year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt. Aaron was 123 years old when he died on Mount Hor” (verses 38-39).

The list ends at the present camp, on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho (verses 48-49).
passages.hearers:
The book is nearly finished. Before Israel crosses the river, it stops to look back over the whole road. Forty years are gathered into one chapter.

Lists like this were a known form in the ancient world. Assyrian kings recorded their campaigns stage by stage in the same manner, and Egyptian texts list the stops along a route. This is one of the few places in the five books of Moses where Moses is said in so many words to write.

The Hebrew word for a ‘stage’ comes from a verb that means to pull up tent pegs. Each name on the list is a camp struck and moved. And each move began the same way, when the cloud lifted from the tabernacle (9:17-23).

To a modern reader it is a list of names, many of them unknown. To an Israelite many of the names were stories. Marah was the bitter water. Elim was the twelve springs and the palm trees. Rephidim was the thirst. Kibroth-hattaavah was the graves of craving. To hear the list read was to walk the road again.

Notice what the list leaves out. It does not mention the golden calf. It says nothing of the scouts, or Korah, or the snakes. The great failures of the wilderness are passed over in silence. The notes that break the rhythm are about other things: the leaving of Egypt, the sea, the springs, the death of Aaron. This is a record of God's leading. Israel's sins are told elsewhere, and fully. Here the people are simply reminded that they were brought every step of the way.

Much about the route is not known. Some places are well attested: Rameses and Succoth in the eastern Nile delta, and Ezion-geber at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba. Kadesh is often placed at the springs of Ain el-Qudeirat in the northeast of the Sinai Peninsula. Punon is generally identified with Feinan, an old copper-mining area south of the Dead Sea. But many of the names in the middle of the list, from Rithmah to Ezion-geber (verses 18-35), appear nowhere else in the Bible, and most cannot be placed today. Where Mount Sinai stood is itself debated. For these reasons no one has been able to draw the whole route with confidence, and the map on the book page does not try.
passages.later:
Moses told the next generation what the long road had been for: “Remember that these forty years the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart” (Deuteronomy 8:2).

Paul says that the wilderness story was written down for the church: “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

Hebrews describes the people of faith as travelers who ‘were longing for a better country, a heavenly one’ (Hebrews 11:16).
passages.hard:
Why does this list sometimes differ from other accounts of the wilderness road?

A reader who compares the chapter with Exodus, the rest of Numbers and Deuteronomy will notice differences. Some camps named here are not mentioned elsewhere. Some places mentioned elsewhere are not here. Deuteronomy says that Aaron died at Moserah (Deuteronomy 10:6), while this chapter places his death at Mount Hor, several stages after a place called Moseroth.

Scholars explain this in different ways. Some suggest that Moserah was a district that included Mount Hor, or that the lists record different kinds of stopping places. Some think the chapter joins several older lists made at different times. Others think the list is selective and arranged for a purpose of its own.

Because so many of the sites cannot be identified, no reconstruction of the whole route has won agreement, and these notes do not offer one. What the chapter clearly claims is that Israel's road from Egypt to Moab was real, that it was remembered, and that God led it.
passages.asks: Moses was told to write down every stage, the hard places and the pleasant ones alike. Ask what the list of your own life's stages would look like, and where on it you can now see that you were being led. And ask what you remember mostly as failure that God might record simply as a place he brought you through.

passages.happening:
On the plains of Moab God gives Moses a charge for the people. “When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan, you must drive out before you all the inhabitants of the land, destroy all their carved images and cast idols, and demolish all their high places” (verses 51-52).

“You are to take possession of the land and settle in it, for I have given you the land to possess” (verse 53). It is to be divided by lot among the clans (verse 54).

A warning follows. “But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land before you, those you allow to remain will become barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides” (verse 55). “And then I will do to you what I had planned to do to them” (verse 56).
passages.hearers:
The chapter turns from the road behind to the task ahead.

The command names three things that belonged to the worship of Canaan. Carved images and cast idols were figures of gods, kept in shrines and in homes. High places were local sanctuaries, usually on a hill, with an altar. Israel is to remove them. The reason is the one Israel had just learned at Peor, where a shared feast led to the worship of another god and twenty-four thousand deaths. The stress of the command falls on the idols and the shrines.

The verb for what Israel is to do to the people, yarash, means both to take possession of land and to put its occupants out of it. This passage speaks of driving out. It does not use the language of killing.

Verse 56 is easy to pass over, and it governs the whole. Israel is given no special standing that excuses it. If it takes up the ways of the peoples it replaces, God will treat Israel exactly as he treated them. The same measure applies to both. The rest of the Old Testament records that this warning was carried out. Israel and Judah were themselves driven from the land, by Assyria and then by Babylon.

The land is called a gift: ‘I have given you the land’. And it is to be shared out by lot and by need, as chapter 26 laid down, so that no clan can seize the best for itself.

The hard question below takes up what troubles a modern reader about this passage.
passages.later:
The warning came true within a generation. The angel of the LORD said to Israel, “So now I tell you that I will not drive out these people before you; they will be thorns in your sides, and their gods will be a snare to you” (Judges 2:3).

Moses told Israel that the land was no reward for its goodness: “It is not because of your righteousness or uprightness of heart that you are going in to possess their land” (Deuteronomy 9:5).

Leviticus had said the same thing as verse 56 in a harder picture: “if you defile the land, it will vomit you out as it spewed out the nations before you” (Leviticus 18:28).
passages.hard:
How can God command a people to drive others from their land? And does this passage give anyone a claim today?

This passage belongs with the Bible's wider account of the conquest of Canaan, which is among the hardest subjects in Scripture. The moral objection to it is one the Bible itself teaches a reader to feel.

Christians who receive these books as God's word read the conquest in more than one way, as the site's pages on it set out. Some read it as God's judgment on particular peoples after long patience, pointing to God's word to Abraham that ‘the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete’ (Genesis 15:16), and they ground it in God's right over every life. Some read the Bible's sweeping language of conquest as the common idiom of ancient war, and note that Exodus speaks of the peoples being put out ‘little by little’ (Exodus 23:30) and that Joshua and Judges show many of them still living in the land. Some read these texts as God meeting an ancient people within the limits of their understanding, to be read in the light of Christ; others reply that this reading weakens the authority of Scripture. Each reading has a cost, and these notes take no side.

Under all of them certain things hold. The command was tied to one land and one moment in Israel's story. Its stated concern is the worship of other gods. Israel was put under the same judgment and suffered it. The prophets never extended the command, and the New Testament never renews it. Jesus rebuked disciples who wanted fire called down on a village (Luke 9:54-55).

So this passage gives no one a claim today. It names no modern nation, people, border or conflict, and it may not be quoted for or against any. In past centuries Christians did quote the conquest to justify taking land and killing its people, in the Crusades and in the colonies of the Americas. That was a misuse of Scripture, and it was wrong.

No one may use this passage as a reason for violence against any person or people, or for driving anyone from their home.

The site's guide to the violence of the Old Testament, its page on the command to destroy the Canaanites, and the Honest Answer on that question go further.
passages.asks: God told Israel that it would be judged by the same measure as the peoples it replaced. Ask whether you hold yourself, your church and your nation to the standard you apply to others. And ask what ‘high places’ remain in your own life: the small altars to other loyalties that you have never quite removed.
